challenges.name: conflict-resolution-quiz
challenges.title: Read the sync conflicts
challenges.description: Three statements about the conflicts Rice Rocket found once couriers edited deliveries offline while dispatchers edited them on the web. Decide whether each one is true.
hints: Compare the two clocks in the evidence with the real order of events. Who sets `updatedAt`, and how far can that clock be off?
List the fields each side changed. Field-level merge decides fields only one side changed; what is left when both sides changed the same field?
To know whether a value changed on the phone, on the server, or on both, you need one more value than the two copies being merged. Which one?

questions.question:
The sync used last-write-wins on the whole delivery, comparing `updatedAt` set by each writer:

```text
04:12:03 (real time)  dispatcher fixes the address on the web   updatedAt=2026-11-06T04:12:03Z (server clock)
04:14:40 (real time)  courier adds a gate code, offline         updatedAt=2026-11-06T04:07:31Z (phone clock, 7 min slow)
04:20:15 (real time)  phone syncs: server copy is newer -> courier's gate code dropped
```

Statement: "Last-write-wins is safe as long as every writer stores an `updatedAt` timestamp with its change."
questions.explanation: False. The timestamps come from different clocks: the phone's runs 7 minutes slow, so its later edit looks older and is thrown away. A phone clock can be minutes or hours off (manual time, a dead battery, a traveller's time zone handling). Even with perfect clocks, whole-record last-write-wins drops the other side's edits to different fields. Server-assigned versions, a base copy for three-way merge, or hybrid logical clocks avoid trusting device time.

questions.question:
After switching to a per-field merge, one delivery still showed this:

```text
field     base               courier (offline)     dispatcher (web)
address   12 Le Loi, D1      12A Le Loi, D1        14 Le Loi, D1
note      ""                 "gate code 4471"     ""
```

Statement: "With a per-field merge there are no conflicts left, so the app never needs to show one to the courier."
questions.explanation: False. The note changed on one side only and merges cleanly, but both sides changed `address` to different values. The merge has to apply a rule (here the dispatcher's value wins for addresses) and, because the courier's edit is lost, tell the courier. Field-level merge shrinks conflicts to the fields both sides changed; it does not remove them.

True. With only `local` and `remote`, a difference in a field could mean the courier changed it, the dispatcher changed it, or both did. Comparing each side with `base` answers it: equal to base on one side means only the other side changed it. That is the three-way merge git uses for text, applied per field. The cost is storing the base copy until the edit syncs.

challenges.name: three-way-delivery-merge
challenges.title: Merge an offline edit with the dispatcher's changes
challenges.description: When an offline courier comes back online, the app merges the courier's copy of a delivery with the api's current copy, field by field, using `base`, the version the edit started from. The first version trusted the newest `updatedAt` (and phone clocks are wrong), let the api's copy override the courier's own edits, and doubled list items. The editor holds `mergeDelivery` with its key blocks missing, each marked by a `// [ ]` line; some pieces are wrong on purpose. Fill every line so that: a field only one side changed takes that side's value; a field both changed to the same value keeps it; a field both changed differently follows its policy (`server`: the api's value, reported in `conflicts`; `device`: the courier's; `union`: each list item once, sorted); and `updatedAt` never decides anything. Run merges deliveries edited on both sides, including one from a phone whose clock runs fast.
hints: For each field of a test, mark it: changed by the courier, by the dispatcher, by both. Only the last group needs a policy.
Look at which copy each branch returns after comparing with `base`, at whether anything compares `updatedAt`, and at how two lists become one without repeating an item.

Merging a shared shopping list item: `if (same(mine.qty, base.qty)) qty = theirs.qty; else if (same(theirs.qty, base.qty)) qty = mine.qty; else qty = Math.max(mine.qty, theirs.qty)` and labels `[...new Set([...mine.labels, ...theirs.labels])].sort()`.

tests.name: The courier adds a gate code while the dispatcher fixes the address: both survive
Both add tags: each tag kept once
Both change the address: the dispatcher's value wins and the courier is told
A phone clock 10 minutes fast does not make the courier's phone number win
Proof photo kept from the phone; a status both sides set the same way is no conflict
